article_title: CHAPTER 8 ‒ Assessing Persistence in Educational Games
citation: Ventura, M., Shute, V., & Small, M. (2013). Assessing Persistence in Educational Games. Design Recommendations for Intelligent Tutoring Systems - Volume 2: Adaptive Instructional Management. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Assessing+Persistence+in+Educational+Games
title: NP session event logs as embedded assessment data
description: Newton's Playground automatically records detailed gameplay telemetry for assessment purposes. "NP automatically uploads log files to a server for each gaming session (i.e., log activity between login and logout)." Each event log for a puzzle visit records features such as game_time, pause_time, restart_count, object_count, nudge_count, erase_count, pin_count, agent vectors, ball trajectory, silver and gold trophy status, and whether the problem was solved. These logs supplied the raw data from which the game-based assessment of persistence was derived.
requirements: Log files must be uploaded to a server for each gaming session between login and logout
target_learning_goals: stealth assessment of persistence during gameplay
examples: The chapter prints a sample event log showing game_time of 130.526001 seconds, restart_count of 7, and solved: true
key_sources: Ventura, M., Shute, V., & Small, M. (2013). Assessing Persistence in Educational Games. Design Recommendations for Intelligent Tutoring Systems - Volume 2: Adaptive Instructional Management. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Assessing+Persistence+in+Educational+Games

article_title: Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference
citation: Catherine Doughty. (1991). Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference: Evidence from an Empirical Study of SL Relativization. SSLA, 13, 431-469. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100010287
title: Noun Phrase Accessibility Hierarchy (NPAH) as predictor of relative clause acquisition difficulty
description: The NPAH is a typological markedness hierarchy ordering relative clause types by accessibility of the relative pronoun's function. The article reports that "the implicational accessibility ordering continues as follows: DIRECT OBJECT, then INDIRECT OBJECT, then OBJECT OF A PREPOSITION, then POSSESSIVE, and finally OBJECT OF A COMPARISON", with SUBJECT relativization universally easiest. It was used to select the instructional sequence and to interpret acquisitional findings from FLA and SLA studies.
requirements: Descriptive and acquisitional research on the target grammatical subsystem to inform sequencing decisions
constraints: The article notes exactly what constitutes difficulty has not yet been clearly established
examples: The study selected OBJECT OF A PREPOSITION relative clauses, a marked position on the hierarchy, as the focus of instruction
key_sources: Catherine Doughty. (1991). Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference: Evidence from an Empirical Study of SL Relativization. SSLA, 13, 431-469. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100010287

article_title: From Policy to Practice: Knowledge gaps and training outcomes related to MASLD guidelines among medical officers in Chhattisgarh, India.
citation: Kaushal Kanica, Aggarwal Priyanka, Saifi Ghazala, Mhatre Siddhesh, Kumar Guresh, Jain Sumi, Shah Urvin Kumar Prafulkumar, Gautam Sumridhi, Sarin Shiv Kumar. (2026). From Policy to Practice: Knowledge gaps and training outcomes related to MASLD guidelines among medical officers in Chhattisgarh, India. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-026-14169-y
title: Monthly NP-NCD reporting and compilation forms (Forms 1–6) for MASLD data across healthcare levels
description: A set of monthly reporting and compilation formats (Forms 1, 2, 2A, 3A, 3B, 4, 5A, 5B, 6) under India's NP-NCD programme, mapping data flow from sub centre through PHC, CHC, district hospital and NCD cells to the national NCD cell, with named responsible officers and fixed submission deadlines. The article states medical officers were "acquainted with a novel monthly reporting and compilation form (Table 1) to ensure systematic data collection, reporting, and referral across all levels of the healthcare system". For example, PHC medical officers compile Form 1 into Forms 2 and 2A and report to the CHC NCD Clinic by the 5th of each month.
requirements: Adoption of the revised reporting templates at facility level, with structured training on MASLD-specific case documentation and referral protocols
constraints: Many health facilities continue using outdated reporting formats despite updated guidelines, hampering proper documentation and monitoring, as the article states
target_learners: Medical officers and NCD nodal officers at sub centre, PHC, CHC, district hospital and state NCD cell levels
target_learning_goals: Systematic MASLD data collection, reporting and referral across all levels of the healthcare system
examples: Table 1 maps each form to its level, data source, responsible person and submission deadline, e.g. Form 2 and 2A compiled by the MO I/c PHC-HWC and due to the CHC NCD Clinic by the 5th of every month
key_sources: Kaushal Kanica, Aggarwal Priyanka, Saifi Ghazala, Mhatre Siddhesh, Kumar Guresh, Jain Sumi, Shah Urvin Kumar Prafulkumar, Gautam Sumridhi, Sarin Shiv Kumar. (2026). From Policy to Practice: Knowledge gaps and training outcomes related to MASLD guidelines among medical officers in Chhattisgarh, India. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-026-14169-y

article_title: Immersive virtual reality training: Addressing challenges and unlocking potentials.
citation: Sohlin AM, Kjærgaard J, Hoffman IM, et al. (2025). Immersive virtual reality training: Addressing challenges and unlocking potentials. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.15748
title: Normalisation process theory as a lens for understanding IVR integration into routine simulation practice
description: The study applies normalisation process theory (NPT) as a theoretical lens for exploring enablers and barriers to integrating IVR simulation into routine practice. NPT "argues that four mechanisms are crucial to determining whether a new intervention becomes successfully integrated into routine practice": coherence, cognitive participation, collective action and reflexive monitoring. The study's five themes (understanding, engagement, strategies in action, appraisal, psychological safety) were mapped onto these NPT domains, with psychological safety spanning all four.
requirements: Analysis must re-engage with inductively derived themes deductively through the NPT constructs
constraints: Applied here to stakeholder perceptions in simulation-based emergency training, not to measured implementation outcomes
target_learning_goals: Understanding implementation of IVR simulation-based training in routine practice
examples: Figure 2 of the article illustrates the four NPT domains, the corresponding research questions, and the five identified themes and subthemes
key_sources: Sohlin AM, Kjærgaard J, Hoffman IM, et al. (2025). Immersive virtual reality training: Addressing challenges and unlocking potentials. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.15748

article_title: Pupilometer efficacy in monitoring anxiety in undergraduate medical students during high-fidelity clinical simulation.
citation: Martín-Rodríguez Francisco et al. (2025). Pupilometer efficacy in monitoring anxiety in undergraduate medical students during high-fidelity clinical simulation. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-95290-6
title: Digital pupillometer (NPi-300) as a repeatable, noninvasive physiological measure of simulation-induced anxiety
description: The NPi-300 Pupillometer (NeurOptics) was used to measure pupillary response before and after simulated clinical scenarios in sixth-year medical students. The article positions pupillometry against questionnaire-based anxiety measurement, noting that "pupillometry allows for consecutive application as many times as deemed necessary, as it is a noninvasive technique with an extremely easy training curve for providers". It recorded maximum diameter, max/min difference, constriction velocity, and dilation velocity for both eyes.
requirements: Measurements must be taken under controlled, identical environmental conditions, since ambient light and near-focus adjustments can alter pupil size
constraints: Pupillometer measurements can be influenced by the light reflex and the near reflex, so lighting variations may provoke significant changes in pupil size
target_learning_goals: monitoring anxiety during high-fidelity clinical simulation to enable personalized tutoring
examples: Pre- and postsimulation pupillary measurements in the same laboratory under identical environmental conditions for all 61 participants
key_sources: Martín-Rodríguez Francisco et al. (2025). Pupilometer efficacy in monitoring anxiety in undergraduate medical students during high-fidelity clinical simulation. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-95290-6

article_title: Benefits of a near-peer program from the tutors' perspective: a survey of Australian junior doctors in a regional teaching program.
citation: Medveczky D, Mitchell A, Leopardi E, Dawson A. (2025). Benefits of a near-peer program from the tutors’ perspective: a survey of Australian junior doctors in a regional teaching program. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06762-2
title: Near-Peer Medical Teaching (NPMT) program: a flexible junior-doctor-led near-peer teaching program with an online repository of consultant-reviewed lesson plans and an annual teaching skills workshop
description: The NPMT program at the Central Coast Clinical School (University of Newcastle) is designed and facilitated by junior doctors (interns and residents) for medical students, offering bedside teaching, small-group tutorials and simulated skills sessions in Medicine, Surgery and Critical Care. Participation is flexible, "delivering anywhere from a single skill session to regular weekly bedside teaching", allowing self-management of workload. Support includes an online repository (npmteaching.com.au) with "consultant-reviewed lesson plans" and an annual teaching skills workshop. Approximately 50–75 tutors are active at any one time.
requirements: Junior doctor tutors volunteering alongside clinical duties; teaching support via the online repository and annual teaching skills workshop
constraints: Teaching occurs within a working environment with competing clinical responsibilities; participation is flexible without a pre-established requirement of commitment
target_learners: Medical students on clinical placements at Gosford and Wyong hospitals
target_learning_goals: Clinical knowledge and skills in Medicine, Surgery and Critical Care disciplines
examples: Founded in 2016; one third to half of each annual junior doctor cohort chooses to participate; tutors accessed an on-demand online repository of teaching resources
key_sources: Medveczky D, Mitchell A, Leopardi E, Dawson A. (2025). Benefits of a near-peer program from the tutors’ perspective: a survey of Australian junior doctors in a regional teaching program. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06762-2

article_title: Implementing e-learning and e-tools for care home staff supporting residents with dementia and challenging behaviour: A process evaluation of the ResCare study using normalisation process theory.
citation: Keenan Julia, Poland Fiona, Manthorpe Jill, Hart Cathryn, Moniz-Cook Esme. (2018). Implementing e-learning and e-tools for care home staff supporting residents with dementia and challenging behaviour: A process evaluation of the ResCare study using normalisation process theory. Dementia. https://doi.org/10.1177/1471301218803195
title: Normalisation process theory (NPT) as a four-construct framework for understanding implementation of complex interventions
description: Normalisation process theory explains how new practices become embedded (normalised) in routine work. The article uses NPT to structure collection, coding and interpretation of interview and process data, examining what staff do individually and collectively to embed the intervention. It is built around four constructs of social action: "the ways that people make sense of the practice (‘Coherence’)", cognitive participation, collective action, and reflexive monitoring. NPT was originally developed to explain why eHealth initiatives failed to become routine practice, making it apt for this e-learning intervention.
requirements: Data on implementation processes across the phases of an intervention, including interview and documentary process data
constraints: The authors note that, as with other users of NPT, they missed the perspectives of residents and of staff who did not attend the training
target_learners: care home staff implementing new practices
service improvers and researchers implementing complex interventions
target_learning_goals: understanding and embedding new ways of working in routine practice
examples: The study used NPT to link contextual data, process and outcome data for 27 intervention homes and to structure interviews in four case study homes
key_sources: Keenan Julia, Poland Fiona, Manthorpe Jill, Hart Cathryn, Moniz-Cook Esme. (2018). Implementing e-learning and e-tools for care home staff supporting residents with dementia and challenging behaviour: A process evaluation of the ResCare study using normalisation process theory. Dementia. https://doi.org/10.1177/1471301218803195

article_title: IMPlementation of An online Relatives' Toolkit for psychosis or bipolar (IMPART study): iterative multiple case study to identify key factors impacting on staff uptake and use.
citation: Lobban Fiona, Appelbe Duncan, Appleton Victoria, Billsborough Julie, Fisher Naomi Ruth, Foster Sheena, Gill Bethany, Glentworth David, Harrop Chris, Johnson Sonia, Jones Steven H., Kovacs Tibor Zoltan, Lewis Elizabeth, Mezes Barbara, Morton Charlotte, Murray Elizabeth, O'Hanlon Puffin, Pinfold Vanessa, Rycroft-Malone Jo, Siddle Ronald, Smith Jo, Sutton Chris J., Viglienghi Pietro, Walker Andrew. (2020). IMPLementation of An online Relatives' Toolkit for psychosis or bipolar (IMPART study): iterative multiple case study to identify key factors impacting on staff uptake and use. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-020-5002-4
title: Normalisation Process Theory as an organising framework for analysing digital health intervention implementation
description: Normalisation Process Theory (NPT) focuses on "the work done by staff to understand the processes by which a complex healthcare intervention is implemented, embedded, and integrated (or not) into practice". The IMPART study used NPT's four core constructs — coherence, cognitive participation, collective action, and reflexive monitoring — to structure data collection, qualitative framework analysis and interpretation of factors affecting REACT uptake. The authors report NPT proved a useful framework and note it has been extensively applied in eHealth settings, allowing comparison with previous studies.
requirements: Data collection, analysis and interpretation are guided by the four NPT constructs, with qualitative data synthesised against them
constraints: The article notes many alternative theoretical frameworks could have been used, and names the NASSS framework as possibly more useful for future DHI-specific work
target_learners: clinical staff in mental health services implementing digital health interventions
target_learning_goals: embedding a digital health intervention into routine clinical practice
examples: Qualitative data from each case were synthesised using the four main constructs of NPT, with coding frameworks discussed in multi-disciplinary data clinics

article_title: Students as anatomy near-peer teachers: a double-edged sword for an ancient skill.
citation: Dickman N, Barash A, Reis S, Karasik D. (2017). Students as anatomy near-peer teachers: a double-edged sword for an ancient skill. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0996-y
title: Near-peer instructor training program combining didactics, cooperative reciprocal peer teaching, and hands-on prosection
description: An eight-session elective training program, run at the end of the second semester or start of summer break, that prepares top first-year anatomy students (grade 85/100 or above) to assist dissection teaching the following year. Content includes "the basics of didactics and pedagogic approaches and teaching methods", constructivist learning theory, active learning, facilitation skills, reflective writing, feedback methods, and advanced cadaveric dissection. The program is "based on a principle of cooperative learning, with reciprocal peer teaching, where students alternate roles as teacher and student", with peer evaluations via student-developed rubrics and a culminating CBL session or mini-lecture plus prosection.
requirements: Participants are selected from students who graduated their anatomy class with a grade of 85 (out of 100) or above
Providing ongoing verbal and written peer evaluations was a requirement for the participants
constraints: Due to financial restraints, only the top training program graduates (four to six annually) could be employed as NPIs
examples: Twelve to fifteen students attended annually in 2013–2015; each presented a case-based learning session or mini-lecture and performed a prosection evaluated by peers using a questionnaire.
key_sources: Dickman N, Barash A, Reis S, Karasik D. (2017). Students as anatomy near-peer teachers: a double-edged sword for an ancient skill. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0996-y
